Acceleration.Definition: The change in an object's velocity divided by the time it took to make that change; equal to the derivative (slope) of an object's velocity–time function.

Amplitude.Definition: The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position during a cycle of periodic motion; also, the height of a wave.

Angular momentum.Definition: The amount of effort it would take to make a rotating object stop spinning.

Atom.Definition: The fundamental unit of matter; includes protons and neutrons in a small nucleus, surrounded by electrons.

Atomic mass unit (amu).Definition: The mass of a proton; also the mass of a neutron.

Average speed.Definition: The distance an object travels divided by the time it took to travel that distance.

Capacitor.Definition: A charge-storage device, often used in circuits.

Centrifugal force.Definition: A made-up force; when discussing circular motion, only talk about “centripetal” forces.

Centripetal force.Definition: The force keeping an object in uniform circular motion.

Coefficient of friction.Definition: The ratio of the friction force to the normal force. The coefficient of static friction is used when an object has no velocity relative to the surface it is in contact with; the coefficient of kinetic friction is used for a moving object.

Concave lens.Definition: A translucent object that makes the light rays passing through it diverge.

Conservative force.Definition: A force that acts on an object without causing the dissipation of that object's energy in the form of heat.

Current.Definition: The flow of positive charge in a circuit; the amount of charge passing a given point per unit time.

Dipole.Definition: Something, usually a set of charges, with two nonidentical ends.

Displacement.Definition: A vector quantity describing how far an object moved.

Elastic collision.Definition: A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved.

Electric field.Definition: A property of a region of space that affects charged objects in that particular region.

Electric flux.Definition: The amount of electric field that penetrates a certain area.

Electric potential.Definition: Potential energy provided by an electric field per unit charge.

Electromagnetic induction.Definition: The production of a current by a changing magnetic field.

Electron.Definition: A subatomic particle that carries a negative charge.

Equilibrium.Definition: When the net force and net torque on an object equal zero.

Equipotential lines.Definition: Lines that illustrate every point at which a charged particle would experience a given potential.

Field.Definition: A property of a region of space that can affect objects found in that particular region.

Free-body diagram.Definition: A picture that represents one or more objects, along with the forces acting on those objects.

Frequency.Definition: The number of cycles per second of periodic motion; also, the number of wavelengths of a wave passing a certain point per second.

Friction.Definition: A force acting parallel to two surfaces in contact; if an object moves, the friction force always acts opposite the direction of motion.

Fulcrum.Definition: The point about which an object rotates.

g.Definition: Free-fall acceleration near the Earth's surface, about 10 m/s2.

Induced EMF.Definition: The potential difference created by a changing magnetic flux that causes a current to flow in a wire; EMF stands for “electro- motive force,” but the units of EMF are volts..

Inductance.Definition: The property of an inductor that describes how good it is at resisting changes in current in a circuit.

Inductor.Definition: A coil in a circuit that makes use of induced EMF to resist changes in current in the circuit.

Inelastic collision.Definition: A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved, as opposed to an elastic collision, in which the total kinetic energy of all objects is the same before and after the collision.

Inertia.Definition: The tendency for a massive object to resist a change in its velocity.

Internal energy.Definition: The sum of the kinetic energies of each molecule of a substance.

Ion.Definition: An electrically charged atom or molecule.

Kirchoff's laws.Definition: In a circuit, 1) at any junction, the current entering equals the current leaving; 2) the sum of the voltages around a closed loop is zero.

Lenz's law.Definition: The direction of the current induced by a changing magnetic flux creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux.

Magnetic field.Definition: A property of a region of space that causes magnets and moving charges to experience a force.

Magnetic flux.Definition: The amount of magnetic field that penetrates an area.

Magnitude.Definition: How much of a quantity is present; see “scalar” and “vector”.

Mass spectrometer.Definition: A device used to determine the mass of a particle.

Momentum.Definition: The amount of “oomph” an object has in a collision, equal to an object's mass multiplied by that object's velocity.

Net force.Definition: The vector sum of all the forces acting on an object.

Normal force.Definition: A force that acts perpendicular to the surface on which an object rests.

Nucleus.Definition: The small, dense core of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.

Oscillation.Definition: Motion of an object that regularly repeats itself over the same path.

Parallel.Definition: The arrangement of elements in a circuit so that the charge that flows through one element does not flow through the others.

Perfectly inelastic collision.Definition: A collision in which the colliding objects stick together after impact.

Period.Definition: The time it takes for an object to pass through one cycle of periodic motion; also, the time for a wave to propagate by a distance of one wavelength.

Power.Definition: The amount of work done divided by the time it took to do that work; also, in a circuit, equal to the product of the current flowing through a resistor and the voltage drop across that resistor.

Resistance.Definition: A property of a circuit that resists the flow of current.

Resistor.Definition: Something put in a circuit to increase its resistance.

Restoring force.Definition: A force that restores an oscillating object to its equilibrium position.

Scalar.Definition: A quantity that has a magnitude but no direction.

Series.Definition: The arrangement of elements in a circuit so that they are connected in a line, one after the other.

Time constant.Definition: A value related to how long it takes to charge or discharge a capacitor, or for current to flow in an inductor.

Torque.Definition: The application of a force at some distance from a fulcrum; if the net torque on an object isn't zero, the object's rotational velocity will change.

Vector.Definition: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.

Velocity.Definition: How fast an object's displacement changes; equal to the derivative (slope) of an object's position–time function.

Weight.Definition: The force due to gravity; equal to the mass of an object times g, the gravitational field.

Work.Definition: The product of the distance an object travels and the components of the force acting on that object directed parallel to the object's direction of motion.

Work-energy theorem.Definition: The net work done on an object equals that object's change in kinetic energy.
